title: Remembering
hook: a run in a friend's name, and an old sutta about gifts that reach the dead
tomorrow: what do you bring into a room where someone is dying?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a warm mug in both hands: breath underneath, kindness around. Held gently. Today, what love does next, when there's nobody left to hand the mug to.

People find ways to keep giving after someone dies. A run in a friend's name. A donation to the cause a grandmother loved. A favorite dish cooked on the day they died, every year. So can you still give someone a gift after they've gone, or is it only for the people left behind? A short Buddhist text answers yes, and families still chant it at memorials. It doesn't start with rules or rituals. It opens with a strange, tender picture: the dead, coming back to their old homes, standing outside the walls.
screen: `A RUN IN A FRIEND'S NAME.` → `CAN A GIFT STILL REACH THEM?` → `STANDING OUTSIDE THE WALLS.`

segments.voice: The text is called the discourse outside the walls. It pictures the departed waiting at crossroads and doorposts of the houses they knew, hoping their families remember them. Then it says something blunt: weeping and sorrow and lament don't help the dead. What helps is giving. When a family gives food, drink or cloth to the community of monks and nuns, and dedicates the good of it to the one who died, the text says the gift reaches them, and they rejoice. Buddhists call this sharing merit. The good you do isn't a coin you keep; it can be passed on. The text even gives the words a family says as they give: idam vo ñatinam hotu, sukhita hontu ñatayo. May this be for our relatives; may our relatives be happy. Around Buddhist Asia this takes many forms. A Thai family offers a meal to monks in a grandfather's name. A Vietnamese family keeps the giỗ, a death anniversary, with incense and a favorite dish. And there's a quiet second gift inside it. The text closes by saying the dead have been honored, and the giver has gained no small merit. Remembering stops being only an ache, a thing that happens to you on bad days. It becomes something you can do for them, with your own two hands.
screen: `THE DEAD OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · `WEEPING DOESN'T REACH THEM.` · `GIVING, DEDICATED TO THEM.` · `MAY OUR RELATIVES BE HAPPY.` · then, large: `FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who has died, or a stranger whose death you heard about this week. Offer this sit to them: breathe, and let each breath be a small gift in their name. At the end, say the old line out loud, in Pali or in English: may this be for them; may they be happy.
Remembering: giving in someone's name after they've died, and sharing the good of it with them. Grief with something to do.
Carry it: for them, because a gift with their name on it still counts. Day eighteen of thirty, offered.

howItsDone: Theravada families offer food or robes to monks and dedicate the merit to the dead, often pouring water as the Tirokudda verses are chanted; Vietnamese families keep the giỗ, a yearly death anniversary, with incense, the person's favorite food and a visit to the temple.

Tirokudda Sutta paraphrased; confirm the details (crossroads, doorposts; lament doesn't help; gifts to the Sangha dedicated to relatives reach them). The Pali dedication line 'idam vo ñatinam hotu, sukhita hontu ñatayo' is written without full diacritics (idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotu, sukhitā hontu ñātayo); confirm.

'Chanted at memorials to this day' and the howItsDone water-pouring detail: common Theravada practice; confirm wording. Giỗ as a Vietnamese custom blends Buddhist and ancestral practice; the script describes it, it doesn't say it is drawn from the sutta.
Chè (a Vietnamese sweet dessert soup) in the chat is not glossed because it's not in the spoken text.
